Determine when order-service quote timeouts actually began (first error/latency deviation, not just report time) and whether pricing-engine p99 ~2.6s started at the same moment or earlier. Enumerate ALL services showing error-rate/latency anomalies in the window 2026-05-20T11:00Z-14:00Z. Extract the exact error signatures on order-service quote failures (timeout vs 5xx vs serialization/deserialization errors, and which downstream call is timing out) and on pricing-engine. Report whether pricing-engine's latency is resource-driven (CPU/mem/GC/connection-pool trend) or call-path-driven.

Find everything that changed in the window 2026-05-20T11:00Z-14:00Z across ALL services (not just market-data-service): deployments, config changes, feature flags. Specifically: (1) the market-data-service serialization change — exact timestamp, scope, what serialization format/dependency it touched; (2) any change to pricing-engine, order-service, or their shared dependencies. Also map the service dependency graph: what order-service calls at the quote step, what pricing-engine and market-data-service depend on, and whether they share a component (datastore, cache, queue, gateway, library). Search historical incidents for prior quote-timeout / pricing-engine p99 spikes to find precedents and known root causes.

Correlate the change timeline against the onset time established in task a. For each change found in task b, state whether its timestamp precedes the observed onset of order-service timeouts and whether it plausibly sits on the failing call path. Decide the most likely fault service and explicitly test the reporter's suspicion: does the market-data-service serialization change timestamp actually align with onset, or does it lag/precede by too much? Test of reporter's suspicion: the market-data-service serialization change (dep-6111, 11:56:00Z) precedes the 12:04:00Z onset by exactly 8 minutes and does NOT align with onset — T1 established the first anomalies in the 12:04Z bucket (pricing-engine WARN 12:05:21Z, order-service first timeout 12:06:10Z). A change 8 min before onset with no market-data-service telemetry anomaly is not temporally consistent with being the trigger.

Contradicting evidence against the market-data-service hypothesis: market-data-service (which sits downstream of pricing-engine on the quote path) shows NO error/latency anomaly in 11:00-12:20Z (only an unrelated TLS WARN 11:43:53Z, zero ERRORs), and order-service's failures are all 'pricing-engine quote call timed out', not serialization/deserialization errors — so the failing downstream edge is order-service -> pricing-engine, not the serialization boundary at pricing-engine -> market-data-service.

The pricing-engine flag ramp cfg-3120 is the only change whose timestamp coincides exactly with the onset bucket: changed_at 12:04:00Z equals the 12:04Z bucket in which T1/F3 found pricing-engine latency_p99 jump ~59-61ms -> 2291ms and F4 found cpu_pct 39-41% -> 91.5-100%, with pricing-engine's own first WARN at 12:05:21Z ('GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took ~3000-8900ms'). The flag author/description flags it as the Greeks v2 ramp, matching the calculator named in the warnings.

Call-path placement: on the quote path order-service -> pricing-engine (http) -> market-data-service (http), pricing-engine is the direct callee of order-service and the caller of market-data-service; pricing-engine and market-data-service share redis-cache. cfg-3120 sits squarely on the failing path (pricing-engine's quote/Greeks computation); dep-6111 sits one hop further downstream and only affects the pricing-engine->market-data-service edge.

Historical precedent HIST-113 (2026-01-28, pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open, symptoms 'quote timeouts','cpu 99%', root cause record market-open volume exceeding capacity) is the closest match by symptom to this incident — but it is a lead, not evidence: HIST-113 attributes the CPU saturation to market-open volume, whereas here the saturation coincides with a Greeks v2 rollout flag, not with a market-open time.

events.answer: The onset bucket is 12:04:00Z. The pricing-engine flag ramp cfg-3120 (greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5→100) is timestamped 12:04:00Z — exactly the onset bucket, and is the only change that lands there. The market-data-service serialization deploy dep-6111 is at 11:56:00Z, 8 minutes BEFORE onset; the reporter's suspicion is not supported: the serialization change neither precedes nor aligns with onset (it is far too early) and market-data-service shows zero errors/anomalies. Most likely fault service: pricing-engine, driven by the Greeks v2 rollout turning on a CPU-heavy Monte-Carlo path that saturates CPU and causes order-service quote timeouts. Ranked hypothesis: (1) cfg-3120 Greek v2 ramp → CPU saturation (strong evidence); (2) dep-6111 protobuf serialization (weak/refuted); (3) capacity/volume (plausible per HIST-113 but no volume signal observed, and timing matches a change, not market open).

events.title: Greeks v2 rollout flag ramp to 100% saturates pricing-engine CPU, stalling quote computation
market-data-service protobuf serialization change (reporter's suspicion) broke/slowed the quote path
Shared redis-cache / exchange-gateway degradation on the shared quote path
Capacity saturation: market-open/volume-driven load exceeding pricing-engine provisioned capacity

events.summary: H1 (Greeks v2 flag ramp → pricing-engine CPU saturation → order-service quote timeouts) is well grounded: onset is firmly pinned to the 12:04Z bucket (F3/F4/F5), cfg-3120 lands exactly there (F8/F16), and pricing-engine's own logs independently show the GreeksV2 20000-path Monte-Carlo path running slow and its own errors are GreeksV2 deadline-exceeded (F2) — not a serialization error. H2 is properly refuted (F6/F15/timing) and H3 is adequately contradicted (F4 shows CPU-bound, not I/O; no shared-component anomaly). The blocking gap is that the leading alternative origin, H4 (organic capacity/market-open load), names a DIFFERENT origin and fix (add capacity vs roll back flag) and was never tested — pricing-engine request_rate was never sampled, so we cannot tell "the code path got more expensive" from "more load arrived," even though a strong historical precedent (HIST-113) matches H4's symptom exactly. One cheap metric query separates them decisively. If request_rate is flat across 11:56→12:04Z while CPU jumps, H1 is confirmed and H4 is killed; if request_rate spiked, the ranking flips. Redis-cache/exchange-gateway health also remains unverified for H3.

events.objective: Sample pricing-engine and order-service request_rate / requests-per-second over 2026-05-20T11:50Z–13:59Z, keyed per bucket. Report explicitly whether pricing-engine request volume spiked at the 12:04Z bucket or stayed flat across the 11:56→12:04Z transition while CPU jumped 40%→99%. Also report order-service request_rate over the same window. This is the decisive discriminator between H1 (code-path cost from the Greeks v2 flag ramp) and H4 (organic volume / market-open capacity saturation with HIST-113 precedent) — a flat request rate with a CPU jump confirms H1 and kills H4; a spike flips the ranking.

Check redis-cache and exchange-gateway health across 2026-05-20T11:50Z–13:59Z: latency, error rate, CPU, and connection saturation. Report whether either shared dependency was degraded at the 12:04Z onset. This directly tests H3 (shared-dependency degradation) rather than dismissing it.

events.statement: pricing-engine request_rate did NOT spike at the 12:04Z onset bucket: at 120s resolution it reads 623.65 (11:56Z), 606.28 (11:58Z), 647.20 (12:00Z), 667.24 (12:02Z), 625.14 (12:04Z), 666.82 (12:06Z) req/s — i.e. the 12:04Z bucket (625.14) is BELOW the preceding 12:02Z bucket (667.24) and within the baseline noise band.

pricing-engine request_rate is flat across the whole 11:50–13:59Z window: 180s buckets range only 582.43–741.12 req/s, mean 646.11, with no step at 12:04Z (12:02Z avg 653.76, 12:05Z avg 652.37, 12:08Z 634.18); the post-onset level equals the pre-onset level.

In the SAME 12:04Z bucket where pricing-engine request_rate was flat (625.14), cpu_pct jumped from a 38-41% baseline to avg 68.44 / max 98.65, then 98.67-99.56 for the rest of the window — a pure CPU-cost step with no corresponding request volume change.

order-service request_rate over the same 11:50–13:59Z window is flat and shows no step at 12:04Z: the 12:02Z bucket avg 239.82 vs the 12:05Z bucket avg 231.73, and the overall range is only 216.83–256.97 req/s (mean 233.06) — no capacity ramp on the caller side either.

Discriminator verdict: a flat request rate coinciding with a 40%→99% CPU jump confirms H1 (fixed code-path cost per request from the Greeks v2 rollout) and is inconsistent with H4 (organic volume / market-open capacity saturation), which requires a request-volume spike that is absent from both pricing-engine and order-service.

events.description: No gap in metric coverage for the decisive signals: both request_rate queries returned partial:false with missing_points:0 (pricing-engine total_points 130, order-service total_points 130).

events.answer: Decisive for H1 over H4: pricing-engine request_rate stayed FLAT across the 11:56→12:04Z transition (~606-667 req/s before, 625 req/s at the 12:04Z bucket, ~642 mean over the whole window) while cpu_pct jumped 40.13%→68.44% avg / 98.65% max in that same 12:04Z bucket and held ~98.7-99.6%. No volume ramp precedes or coincides with the CPU jump. order-service request_rate is likewise flat ~233 req/s (216-257) with no step at 12:04Z. This kills H4 (organic volume / market-open capacity saturation) and confirms H1 (code-path cost from the Greeks v2 flag ramp).

No error/critical log evidence from either shared dependency in 11:50-13:59Z: redis-cache returned exactly 1 WARN total ('deprecated TLS cipher offered by client 46e36f97' at 13:28:54Z) and exchange-gateway exactly 1 WARN ('clock drift 38ms detected, resyncing with NTP' at 12:54:21Z), both truncated:false and neither at or near the 12:04Z onset.

exchange-gateway exposes error_rate, upstream_error_rate, upstream_latency_ms, request_rate, restarts, cpu_pct and memory_pct (confirmed via its available_metrics), so full error-rate/CPU/upstream checks were possible in principle — but those follow-up queries returned budget_exhausted and were never executed.

events.answer: Neither shared dependency was degraded at the 12:04Z onset. redis-cache shows no anomaly in any metric it exposes (cpu_pct 22.0% avg at 12:02Z vs 22.31% at 11:50Z baseline; connected_clients 310-319, well inside the 283-349 band; hit_ratio 96.4%->96.0%; evictions 3.32->2.98/min) and no errors in 11:50-13:59Z. exchange-gateway's latency_p99_ms is flat at ~129-134ms through the onset (mean 130.43ms across the whole window), also with no errors. This evidence argues against H3 (shared-dependency degradation) and leaves pricing-engine's own CPU saturation (H1/H4) as the candidate.

events.title: Greeks v2 rollout flag ramp to 100% saturates pricing-engine CPU, stalling quote computation
Capacity saturation: market-open/volume-driven load exceeding pricing-engine provisioned capacity
Shared redis-cache / exchange-gateway degradation on the shared quote path
market-data-service protobuf serialization change (reporter's suspicion) broke/slowed the quote path

events.summary: H1 is now adequately proven and the leading alternatives are positively contradicted by measured data. Onset is pinned to the 12:04Z bucket (F3/F4/F5: pricing-engine latency 59-61ms→~2.6s, cpu 39-41%→99%, order-service error_rate 0.2%→8%), and the only change landing exactly there is cfg-3120 (greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5→100, F8/F16). The round-1 blocking gap — H4 (organic volume/capacity) vs H1 (code-path cost) — is decisively resolved: pricing-engine request_rate is flat across 11:56→12:04Z (625.14 at the onset bucket vs 667.24 preceding; partial:false, missing_points:0) and order-service is likewise flat, yet CPU steps 40%→99% in the same bucket (F19-F23). No volume spike exists, so H4's required mechanism is absent. H3 is now positively tested, not merely assumed: redis-cache CPU/clients/hit-ratio/evictions are flat and exchange-gateway latency is flat with zero component errors (F25-F29, T5), and pricing-engine is CPU-bound with flat memory (F4), ruling out I/O-blocking shared-dependency degradation. H2 (the reporter's serialization suspicion) is refuted on timing (8 min early), missing telemetry anomaly, and error signature (timeouts, not serialization). Each hop of H1's chain rests on a verified finding except the single declared inference that the flag ramp actually enabled the heavy Monte-Carlo path — a strong inference from F2/F16 that names no competing origin, and whose fix (roll back cfg-3120) is identical under any flag→CPU mechanism. Residual uncertainty (flag→cost not code-inspected; no rollback/intervention test recorded; sub-minute flag-apply ordering rests on log timestamps in a 480s bucket) caps confidence rather than changing the ranking. No failed or truncated result underlies a decisive finding.
